title: Book 9 — Calliope, Chapter 41
paragraphs: For ten days nothing more was done than this; but when the eleventh day came, while they still sat opposite one another at Plataea, the Greeks by now having grown much more numerous and Mardonius being greatly vexed at the delay, Mardonius son of Gobryas and Artabazos son of Pharnakes — a man esteemed by Xerxes above almost all Persians — came to speak with each other. In their discussion, the opinions expressed were these. Artabazos's opinion was that they must set the whole army in motion as soon as possible and move to the walls of the Thebans, where great stores of grain had been brought in for them and fodder for their beasts; there they should settle quietly and get their business done as follows. They had, he said, great quantities of gold (both coined and uncoined) as well as silver and drinking cups, and he advised that these should be sent around without stint to the Greeks, especially to those who were leaders in their various cities; these, he said, would speedily surrender their freedom. He advised that they not risk a battle. His opinion, then, was the same as the Thebans', for he too had some true foresight. But Mardonius's opinion was more vehement and more obstinate, and he was by no means disposed to yield; for he said he thought their army far superior to that of the Greeks, and gave as his opinion that they should engage in battle as quickly as possible and not allow them to assemble in still greater numbers than were already gathered. As for the sacrifices of Hegesistratos, they should leave them alone and not try to force a favorable sign, but follow Persian custom and engage in battle.
